description: What the **served** web app may do over IPC. The served app runs on its own origin (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>`), not the shell's own (`http://tauri.localhost`), so Tauri treats it as remote and it needs a capability of its own — and only ever a narrow one: a capability bound to a remote URL hands its permissions to *every* script that runs in that origin (an XSS in the app, or a page that grabbed the port first), so it must not carry a permission that can read the user's files, run a process or reach out to the OS. Exactly two things are granted: five shell commands, which are the app's entire IPC surface (`invokeShell` in `src/lib/runtime-mode.ts`), and `core:event:allow-listen` / `core:event:allow-unlisten`, which `listenShell` needs to subscribe to the shell's menu events. Everything else is withheld on purpose — in particular the `core:default` baseline, which expands to the image plugin (`plugin:image|from_path` is a bare `std::fs::read` with no scope check, so it reads any file on disk), the menu and tray plugins (a remote origin could mint a menu item with the id `quit` or `restart-server`, and `src-tauri/src/shell.rs` dispatches on the raw id), the path plugin (it resolves the user's home directory) and `core:event:allow-emit` (the app only ever listens). The URL pattern cannot name an ephemeral port, so `src-tauri/src/navigation.rs` is the second gate: the webview may only navigate to this run's exact origin, never another loopback port. The store plugin is withheld from **every** origin: `tauri-plugin-store` does no scope check of its own, and the store's `preferences.json` is not an encrypted secret store.
